title: The Economics of Repair
passage:
Many public decisions depend on measurements that appear objective. Yet the choice of what to measure, how to classify cases, and which period to compare already shapes the story that the numbers tell. A single indicator can be useful while still failing to represent the entire system.

Analysts therefore distinguish between a measure and the phenomenon it is meant to represent. They may compare several indicators, inspect unusual cases, and ask what information has been excluded. This does not make quantitative evidence less valuable. On the contrary, it can make numerical evidence more informative by clarifying its limits.

A mature evaluation does not reject measurement because it is imperfect. It uses measurement while keeping the underlying assumptions visible, especially when decisions affect people who are not represented equally in the data.

The title, then, points to a question of method rather than a single answer. The most reliable approach is to distinguish observation from interpretation and to state the limits of the evidence alongside the conclusion.
